metadata.title: Zombie Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Zombie Bottom position in BJJ. Defensive turtle variant with opponent on top. Learn defensive frames, turtle escapes, and guard recovery with 45% escape success rate.

overview:
Zombie Bottom is a defensive turtle position variant where the practitioner is on their hands and knees with the opponent attempting to establish control from the top. This position is characterized by defensive posturing with the head tucked, elbows in, and a focus on preventing back exposure while working toward guard recovery or standing. The name 'Zombie' reflects the characteristic tucked posture and protective positioning, similar to a defensive shell.

This position is fundamentally a transition state rather than a sustainable position - the bottom player must actively work to escape to guard, sweep to top position, or stand up. Remaining static in Zombie Bottom allows the top player to establish dominant back control, crucifix, or front headlock positions. The primary strategic goal is to create space, protect the back, and transition to a more favorable position as quickly as possible.

Zombie Bottom requires excellent defensive awareness, frame management, and timing. Practitioners must balance between staying tight to prevent back exposure while simultaneously creating movement opportunities for escape. The position is common in scrambles, after failed takedowns, or when defending guard passes, making it an essential defensive skill for all levels of BJJ competition.
state_invariants: Bottom player is on hands and knees with chest facing the mat, creating a turtle shell defensive structure with spine curved to protect vulnerable areas
Head is tucked with chin to chest, elbows pulled tight to ribs/hips, knees under hips maintaining a compact defensive ball to minimize attack surfaces
Opponent is on top attempting to establish control through hooks, harnesses, or front headlock positions while bottom player actively defends and seeks escape
Bottom player's weight is distributed across four points (hands and knees) with hips elevated above shoulders, creating base for explosive movement and escape opportunities
prerequisites: Failed guard pass attempt forcing turtle position
Scramble situation from standing or transition
Defensive response to opponent's takedown or control
Loss of guard position requiring immediate defensive posture
key_principles: Keep head tucked with chin to chest to prevent guillotine and front headlock attacks
Maintain tight elbows to ribs/hips to block opponent's hooks and prevent crucifix entries
Create constant small movements to prevent opponent from settling their weight and establishing control
Protect the back at all costs - never allow hooks to be inserted or harness control established
Work immediately toward guard recovery, standing up, or creating scramble opportunities rather than remaining static
Use frames and hand fighting to create space while maintaining defensive structure
Time explosive movements when opponent's weight shifts or commitment creates openings

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent commits weight forward attempting front headlock
Opponent tries to insert hooks or establish back control
Opponent overcommits to one side attempting to flatten
Opponent lifts hips attempting to lock body triangle or hooks

decision_tree.condition: If opponent attempts front headlock or guillotine control
Else if opponent attempts to insert hooks for back control
Else if opponent establishes upper body control (harness/seatbelt)
Else if opponent applies downward pressure to flatten

common_errors.error: Remaining static in turtle position without movement
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to establish secure back control with hooks and harness, leading to rear naked choke or back mount dominance
common_errors.correction: Create constant micro-movements and weight shifts to prevent opponent from settling, immediately work toward escape rather than defensive stalling

common_errors.error: Lifting head up to see opponent's position
common_errors.consequence: Exposes neck to guillotine chokes, front headlock controls, and allows opponent to establish dominant head control
common_errors.correction: Keep chin tucked to chest at all times, use peripheral vision and feel to track opponent's position rather than lifting head

common_errors.error: Widening elbows away from body to create base
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for opponent to insert hooks under armpits leading to crucifix position or back control establishment
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows glued to ribs/hips, create base through leg positioning and core tension rather than arm positioning

common_errors.error: Flattening hips to the mat when pressure is applied
common_errors.consequence: Eliminates all escape opportunities, allows opponent to ride position comfortably, leads to time-wasting and point accumulation
common_errors.correction: Maintain hip elevation even under pressure, use small bridges and shrimps to keep hips mobile and create escape timing

common_errors.error: Attempting explosive escapes without setup or timing
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy, creates larger openings for opponent's attacks, and reduces effectiveness of subsequent escape attempts
common_errors.correction: Create subtle hand fighting and weight manipulation first, then time explosive movements when opponent's base is compromised or weight shifts

common_errors.error: Ignoring opponent's grip and control establishment
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to build strong positional control making escapes progressively more difficult and energy-intensive
common_errors.correction: Immediately hand fight any grip attempts, strip controls before they become established, prioritize grip fighting as primary defensive action

training_drills.name: Turtle Escape Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Partner applies light pressure on turtle position. Bottom player cycles through all escape options (Granby, technical standup, guard recovery, sitout) for 2-minute rounds. Focus on smooth transitions and maintaining defensive structure throughout movements.

training_drills.name: Defensive Turtle Positional Sparring
training_drills.description: Start in Zombie Bottom with opponent in standard top turtle. Bottom player works escapes while top player attempts to establish back control or submissions. Reset when bottom escapes to guard or top achieves back control. Emphasizes realistic timing and decision-making.

training_drills.name: Granby Roll Chain Drill
training_drills.description: From turtle position, practice Granby roll to guard, then immediately return to turtle and repeat in opposite direction. Builds muscle memory for primary escape technique while developing directional awareness and hip mobility.

training_drills.name: Hand Fighting Defense Drill
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to establish various grips (seatbelt, front headlock, overhooks) while bottom player hand fights and strips grips. Focus on preventing control establishment before working escape techniques.

expert_insights.danaher: The turtle position represents a critical junction in the positional hierarchy - it is neither a guard position nor a pinning position, but rather a transitional defensive structure. The fundamental problem with turtle is that it provides no offensive capability while simultaneously exposing the back, which is the most valuable real estate in grappling. When forced into turtle, your primary mechanical objectives are threefold: first, prevent the insertion of hooks which would allow back control establishment; second, deny the opponent head control which enables both front headlock attacks and the leverage needed to break down your structure; and third, create the angular momentum necessary for rotational escapes, particularly the Granby roll which remains the highest-percentage escape mechanism. The successful turtle bottom player understands that this position has a time limit - the longer you remain static, the more opportunities you provide for your opponent to establish dominant control. Movement is not optional; it is the fundamental requirement for survival.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, turtle bottom is where matches get lost if you don't know what you're doing. I see guys stall in turtle thinking they're safe, but you're just giving away time and letting your opponent build a game plan. My approach is simple - never stay in turtle longer than three seconds unless I'm actively working an escape. The Granby roll is money if you time it right, especially when the guy on top commits his weight trying to flatten you out. That's your window. In no-gi, turtle is even more dangerous because of guillotines and front headlocks, so you need to be more aggressive with your hand fighting and escape timing. The reality is turtle should be a flash position - you're either escaping to guard immediately or you're getting your back taken. In my matches, if I end up in turtle, I'm already moving before my opponent can settle. That's the difference between high-level turtle defense and just surviving - you have to attack the escape, not wait for permission.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Turtle bottom in the 10th Planet system is all about the Twister mentality - even when you're in a bad spot, you're looking for unconventional escapes that your opponent isn't expecting. Yeah, the traditional Granby roll works, but we also train a lot of rubber guard entries from turtle, especially the sit-through to lockdown which catches guys off guard. The key thing we emphasize is creating chaos - if you're static in turtle, you're dead. But if you're constantly moving, hand fighting, and threatening weird transitions, you make the top guy hesitate, and that hesitation is your opening. We also use a lot of technical standups combined with rolling entries because in street situations or MMA, staying on your knees is begging for trouble. The Zombie position specifically, we treat it like a loaded spring - you're coiled up tight, protecting everything, but at any moment you can explode into a Granby, shoot for a single leg, or invert into guard. The name 'Zombie' actually comes from that idea - you look dead but you're really just waiting to come back to life with some crazy escape that nobody sees coming.

metadata.title: Zombie | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Zombie position in BJJ. Defensive turtle variation with unique lockdown mechanics. Learn entries, escapes, and transitions. Success rates: 40-65% recovery.

overview:
The Zombie position is a highly specialized defensive posture within the 10th Planet Jiu-Jitsu system, representing a unique variation of the turtle position combined with lockdown mechanics. Named for its distinctive appearance where the bottom practitioner appears to be rising from the ground while maintaining protective frames, the Zombie serves as both an escape mechanism and a transition hub to more advantageous positions. This position emerged from Eddie Bravo's systematic approach to creating defensive structures that can transform into offensive opportunities.

The Zombie is characterized by the bottom practitioner being on their side with one leg locked around the opponent's leg (similar to lockdown mechanics), while using frames and grips to prevent the opponent from establishing dominant control. The top player is typically attempting to pass to side control or take the back, while the bottom player works to recover guard or sweep. This position represents a critical moment in the positional hierarchy where the defender has lost their guard but hasn't yet been fully passed.

Unlike traditional turtle positions where the practitioner curls into a ball, the Zombie position involves active movement, constant reframing, and strategic use of the lockdown to off-balance the opponent. The position's effectiveness lies in its ability to frustrate passing attempts while creating opportunities for guard recovery, sweeps, or even back takes. Understanding the Zombie position is essential for modern no-gi practitioners, particularly those training in the 10th Planet system or facing opponents who utilize deep half guard and lockdown-based games.
state_invariants: Bottom practitioner positioned on their side with hip facing opponent, creating a defensive shell while maintaining mobility through shoulder and hip positioning
One leg (typically the bottom leg) entangled with opponent's leg using lockdown-style grip with foot hooking behind opponent's calf and thigh squeeze active
Near-side arm creating a defensive frame against opponent's chest or shoulder, preventing forward pressure and maintaining space for hip movement
Head and shoulders protected from opponent's crossface attempts through active head positioning and far-side arm control
Top practitioner attempting to flatten bottom player or establish passing grips while dealing with lockdown control restricting their base and mobility
prerequisites: Guard has been partially compromised but full pass not yet achieved
Bottom practitioner able to establish lockdown on one of opponent's legs
Opponent attempting to consolidate passing position or establish side control
Bottom practitioner has maintained frames preventing complete flattening
Sufficient space exists for hip movement and guard recovery attempts
key_principles: Maintain active lockdown tension to restrict opponent's base and prevent them from completing the pass
Use near-side frame to create distance and prevent opponent from driving chest pressure into your upper body
Keep constant hip movement to prevent being flattened - staying on your side is crucial for escape options
Protect your back and neck from opponent's crossface attempts through active head positioning and grip fighting
Create off-balancing opportunities through lockdown stretching and hip pressure to set up sweeps or guard recovery
Time your escape attempts with opponent's weight shifts and base adjustments for maximum effectiveness

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to free their leg from lockdown by posting or pulling back
Opponent drives forward with crossface pressure while leg is locked
Opponent's weight shifts forward attempting to consolidate side control

Opponent pressures head down attempting to flatten your position

decision_tree.condition: If opponent is heavy on your upper body with strong crossface pressure
If opponent is attempting to free their leg from lockdown by posting or pulling
If opponent establishes strong chest-to-chest pressure attempting to flatten you
If opponent creates distance trying to clear lockdown and establish passing grips

common_errors.error: Allowing yourself to be flattened onto your back without maintaining side positioning
common_errors.consequence: Loses all mobility and offensive options, allowing opponent to complete the pass easily to side control or mount
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant hip pressure and shoulder frames to stay on your side - use lockdown tension to prevent flattening and keep shrimping motion active

common_errors.error: Releasing or loosening the lockdown grip prematurely before establishing better position
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately frees their leg and completes the pass with superior base and mobility
common_errors.correction: Maintain lockdown tension throughout transitions - only release when you've secured guard recovery or committed to a sweep with proper grips established

common_errors.error: Failing to protect the head and neck from crossface attempts
common_errors.consequence: Opponent drives crossface across your face, flattens your shoulders, and achieves dominant chest-to-chest control making escapes nearly impossible
common_errors.correction: Keep active head positioning away from crossface pressure, use near-side frame to block opponent's shoulder, and maintain far-side grip fighting to prevent crossface establishment

common_errors.error: Being static and defensive without attempting sweeps or guard recovery
common_errors.consequence: Opponent methodically works to improve position, eventually achieving the pass or back take through sustained pressure and patience
common_errors.correction: Constantly threaten sweeps and guard recovery to keep opponent defensive - use lockdown stretches, hip bumps, and granby movements to create dynamic threats

common_errors.error: Over-committing to sweep attempts without proper setup or timing
common_errors.consequence: Opponent counters the sweep attempt by using your momentum against you, achieving superior position or transitioning to back control
common_errors.correction: Set up sweeps with proper off-balancing through lockdown manipulation - wait for opponent's weight shifts and base adjustments before committing to sweep execution

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to establish double underhooks or bodylock control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent gains complete control of your torso, can easily lift and manipulate your position, leading to inevitable pass or back take
common_errors.correction: Fight aggressively for underhook control, maintain active frames to prevent opponent from connecting their hands, and use lockdown to disrupt their base before they consolidate grips

common_errors.error: Neglecting to create angles and space for hip movement
common_errors.consequence: Position becomes completely static, allowing opponent to methodically break down your defensive structure with sustained pressure
common_errors.correction: Use near-side frame to create space, shrimp your hips to create angles, and time these movements with lockdown stretches to maximize effectiveness and create escape opportunities

training_drills.name: Zombie Position Retention Drill
training_drills.description: Partner starts in passing position with you in Zombie with lockdown established. Partner attempts to flatten you and complete the pass while you maintain side positioning and frames. Focus on constant hip movement, lockdown pressure, and defensive frames. Reset after each successful defense or pass completion.

training_drills.name: Lockdown Sweep Flow Drill
training_drills.description: From Zombie position, practice flowing between Old School Sweep, Electric Chair threat, and Deep Half entries based on partner's reactions. Partner provides progressive resistance, gradually increasing pressure as your timing improves. Emphasize reading partner's weight distribution and base positioning.

training_drills.name: Zombie to Guard Recovery Sequence
training_drills.description: Start in Zombie position with partner attempting various passing attacks. Your goal is to successfully recover full guard (half guard, lockdown, or closed guard) within 30 seconds. Partner uses different passing strategies each round (knee slice, crossface, leg weave, etc.). Track success rate for each passing style encountered.

training_drills.name: Granby Roll Integration Drill
training_drills.description: Practice Granby Roll specifically from Zombie position when opponent applies heavy shoulder pressure. Partner varies between maintaining pressure and following your roll. Focus on smooth technical execution, protecting your back during the roll, and immediately establishing guard upon completion.

expert_insights.danaher: The Zombie position represents an intelligent application of mechanical leverage principles within a defensive context. The lockdown mechanism creates a structural connection that transforms what would typically be a purely defensive posture into a dynamic offensive platform. By restricting the opponent's base through the locked leg, the bottom practitioner fundamentally alters the biomechanical equation - the passer must now solve two problems simultaneously: maintaining balance on a compromised base while attempting to advance position. The genius of this position lies in its ability to create what I call 'defensive offense' - maintaining frames and structure while continuously threatening sweeps and transitions. The key technical element is understanding that the lockdown creates a fulcrum point around which all movements revolve. When the bottom player extends their locked leg, they create a stretching force that disrupts the opponent's weight distribution, opening windows for guard recovery or sweep execution. The most sophisticated practitioners understand that the Zombie is not a static defensive shell but rather a transitional hub where timing and feel determine success more than raw strength or athleticism.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the Zombie position is most effective when you treat it as a temporary stopping point rather than a destination. I've used this extensively against guys trying to pressure pass my lockdown game - it gives you just enough control to reset the engagement on your terms. The reality is that at the highest levels, staying in Zombie for extended periods is dangerous because elite passers will eventually find ways to flatten you or take your back. The winning strategy is to immediately start hunting for the Old School Sweep or Electric Chair transition the moment you establish the lockdown. I've hit Old School Sweeps on world champions from this exact position because they're so focused on completing the pass that they don't properly defend the sweep mechanics. The key competitive insight is recognizing when your opponent is most off-balance - typically when they're trying to free their trapped leg or when they're driving forward with crossface pressure. These are your money moments to attack. Also, don't be afraid to abandon the position if you can't get the sweep - sometimes re-guarding to half guard is the smart play rather than getting stubborn and eating a pass. The Zombie works best as part of a flowing defensive system, not as a position you're trying to win from.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The Zombie is one of those positions that perfectly embodies the 10th Planet philosophy of turning bad positions into opportunities. I developed this as an answer to the problem every lockdown player faces: what do you do when someone's halfway through passing but you've still got their leg locked up? Traditional BJJ would tell you to let go of the lockdown and try to escape, but that's giving up your only control point. The Zombie says, 'No, keep that leg locked and use it as your weapon.' The beautiful thing about this position is that it creates these dilemma situations - if they pull back to free their leg, you Old School Sweep them. If they drive forward to smash you, you hit the Electric Chair or roll to the Truck. If they try to go around, you recover to lockdown or deep half. Every direction they move creates an opportunity for you. The name 'Zombie' comes from how you look when you're doing it right - you're rising up from the bottom position like you're coming back from the dead. It's also a mental game position because passers hate dealing with it. They think they've got you, they're halfway through the pass, and then suddenly they're locked down and defending sweeps. It messes with their confidence and rhythm. The key is being relentless with it - don't just survive, constantly attack with sweeps and transitions until they make a mistake.

metadata.title: Zombie Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Zombie Top position in BJJ. Comprehensive guide covering control strategies, passing sequences, and counter-defenses against the Zombie lockdown system with expert insights.

overview:
Zombie Top is the controlling position against the opponent's Zombie lockdown structure from 10th Planet Jiu-Jitsu. The top player faces a defensive opponent using the lockdown (leg triangle around one leg) combined with an underhook, creating a highly defensive half guard variation. This position requires strategic passing approaches that neutralize the lockdown's power while maintaining top control and avoiding sweeps.

The Zombie Top position emphasizes posture control, crossface pressure, and systematic leg extraction. Unlike traditional half guard top positions, the lockdown creates significant tension on the trapped leg, requiring specialized passing sequences. The top player must balance maintaining control while working methodically to either extract the leg or transition to alternative passing strategies.

Success in Zombie Top depends on recognizing the opponent's defensive structure and selecting appropriate passing sequences. The position offers multiple offensive pathways including pressure-based passes, leg weave entries, and transitions to back control when the opponent's defensive posture breaks down. Understanding the lockdown mechanics and the opponent's available sweeps is essential for maintaining top control.
state_invariants: Top player positioned over opponent in half guard configuration with one leg trapped by opponent's lockdown (leg triangle), maintaining upper body posture and weight distribution through hips
Opponent on their back utilizing lockdown on one leg while maintaining underhook control on same side, creating defensive structure with body turned slightly to side
Top player's trapped leg experiencing tension from lockdown pressure while free leg posts for base, with upper body controlling opponent's head/shoulders through crossface or underhook counters
Opponent's defensive frame includes lockdown control plus underhook grip, attempting to break top player's posture while threatening sweeps from bottom position
prerequisites: Opponent has established Zombie lockdown structure from half guard bottom
Top player has passed opponent's initial guard frames
Top player maintains upper body control (crossface, whizzer, or underhook)
Top player's leg trapped in lockdown triangle configuration
key_principles: Maintain strong crossface or whizzer control to prevent opponent's underhook from dominating position
Keep weight distributed through hips and chest to prevent opponent from creating angles for sweeps
Control opponent's head position to limit mobility and defensive adjustments
Systematically work to extract trapped leg through posture and pressure rather than explosive force
Recognize opponent's sweep attempts early (Old School, Electric Chair) and counter with weight shifts
Use strategic transitions to alternative positions when direct passing becomes stalled
Maintain patient pressure while advancing passing sequences without overcommitting to single approach

Opponent releases lockdown to re-guard - immediately thread leg through and consolidate side control

Opponent attempts to create space with frames - drive weight through chest and smash past guard
Opponent extends underhook too far - counter with own underhook and drive to opposite side

decision_tree.condition: If opponent maintains strong lockdown and underhook with good posture control
If opponent's lockdown begins to loosen or defensive structure weakens
If opponent turns to turtle to escape passing pressure
If opponent attempts sweep (Old School, Electric Chair)

common_errors.error: Attempting explosive leg extraction against tight lockdown
common_errors.consequence: Wasting energy, potential injury to knee/ankle, allowing opponent to maintain defensive structure indefinitely
common_errors.correction: Use systematic pressure and posture adjustments to gradually loosen lockdown before attempting extraction, work passing sequences that don't require immediate leg freedom

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to establish dominant underhook control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent controls posture, creates sweep opportunities, prevents passing progression
common_errors.correction: Immediately counter underhook with crossface or whizzer, fight for head control, prevent opponent from getting chest-to-chest connection

common_errors.error: Maintaining too upright posture in response to lockdown tension
common_errors.consequence: Makes Old School Sweep and other back-takes highly available, loses control of opponent's upper body
common_errors.correction: Drive weight forward through hips and shoulders while maintaining base, use crossface to flatten opponent rather than sitting upright

common_errors.error: Ignoring opponent's knee shield or frame creation
common_errors.consequence: Opponent re-establishes full guard or creates space for more effective defensive structure
common_errors.correction: Control opponent's top knee aggressively, prevent frames from extending, maintain heavy chest pressure throughout passing sequence

common_errors.error: Committing fully to single passing direction without reading opponent's reactions
common_errors.consequence: Opponent anticipates pass, uses momentum against top player, creates sweep opportunities
common_errors.correction: Maintain multiple passing threats, change direction based on opponent's defensive adjustments, use feints to create openings

common_errors.error: Failing to recognize turtle transition opportunities
common_errors.consequence: Missing high-percentage back-take chances when opponent defensively turns away
common_errors.correction: Stay connected during opponent's turtle transition, immediately establish back control hooks or front headlock control

common_errors.error: Overcommitting to submission attempts from top position
common_errors.consequence: Losing top control, allowing opponent to escape or reverse position
common_errors.correction: Prioritize passing progression over submissions, only attack submissions when position is thoroughly consolidated

expert_insights.danaher: The Zombie Top position exemplifies the importance of systematic pressure application over explosive force. The lockdown creates significant mechanical tension on the trapped leg, making forceful extraction counterproductive and energy-intensive. Instead, focus on controlling the opponent's upper body through crossface mechanics while gradually adjusting your hip position to neutralize the lockdown's power. The passing sequence should progress from establishing dominant head control, to flattening the opponent's defensive posture, to creating angles for leg extraction or alternative passing paths. Understanding the biomechanics of how the lockdown generates tension allows you to methodically dismantle the position rather than fighting against it.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, Zombie Top requires patience and strategic decision-making. Many opponents who play the lockdown are comfortable stalling in this position, so you need to be even more comfortable applying sustained pressure without burning energy. I focus heavily on the crossface because it prevents the Old School Sweep and limits their ability to create attacking angles. When the lockdown is extremely tight, I'll often transition my focus to back-takes rather than forcing the pass directly - if they turn to turtle to escape my pressure, that's often a cleaner path to dominant position. Don't get frustrated by the lockdown; treat it as an opportunity to develop your pressure passing and control maintenance against a defensively-oriented opponent.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: As the creator of the Zombie position, I can tell you that top players who understand the system will beat those who don't every time. The lockdown is designed to create a dilemma - if you try to extract your leg forcefully, you play into the sweep mechanics. If you stay passive, the bottom player can work their underhook and create attacking opportunities. The key is active pressure with smart direction. Drive your crossface hard, control the head, and use your free leg positioning to create passing angles. When you feel the lockdown start to loosen, that's when you accelerate the pass. Also, be ready for the turtle transition - many lockdown players will bail to turtle when the pressure gets heavy, and that's your chance to take the back. The Zombie is a complete system from bottom, but it has clear weaknesses when the top player applies the right pressure sequences.
